title: The piece you picked is the faintest block on the strip
goal: Cut a recording into pieces and the piece you are holding, the one Delete takes, is drawn dimmer than the pieces you are not holding. A piece you have already played through is a solid mid grey block; the piece you just picked, before the playhead has moved into it, is a nearly empty dark box with a thin coloured outline round it. So the strongest thing on the strip says how far you have watched, and the faintest thing on it says what is about to be deleted. Make the picked piece the one that reads first.
notes:
REPRODUCED by picture and confirmed in the code, manager pass 2026-09-19 on HEAD e9d6b163, unlocked screen.

The picture: queue/manager/shots/2026-09-19-video-three-pieces.png, lifted from Scripts/playtest/trim-with-pieces-walk.json step 1 (Scripts/playtest-all.sh --no-build trim, 8 passed). Three pieces. The first two are solid mid grey. The third, which is the picked one, is a dark empty box with a thin accent outline, and it reads as a hole in the strip rather than as a highlight.

The code, Sources/Photonz/CutStrip.swift block(isSelected:playedFraction:) around lines 86 to 98. Each block is three layers: a base fill of .primary.opacity(isSelected ? 0.3 : 0.18), then a played overlay across playedFraction of the width which is accent at 0.75 when picked and .primary.opacity(0.55) when not, then a 1.5 point accent strokeBorder only when picked. In a dark window .primary is white, so the numbers come out:
  picked, not yet played   = white 0.30 + a 1.5pt outline
  not picked, played       = white 0.55
That is the whole bug in two numbers. Being picked is worth +0.12 of fill and a hairline; having been played is worth +0.37. The 2026-09-17-video-cutting-trim-pick audit predicted this in its rough list, in its own words, and could not check it because the Mac was locked: "The colour choice is the thing to look at first and the thing least possible to check... It may be too quiet there." It is quieter than that audit thought, because the comparison is not against an unplayed neighbour, it is against a played one.

Why it matters rather than being a nit: CutStrip's own doc comment says "there is no separate clip selection either: the piece under the playhead is the piece you are holding, and Delete drops the one you are looking at". The only thing on screen saying which piece Delete takes is this drawing, and the user's reported flow is cut, pick, delete, save, send.

One related thing from the same audit, NOT a separate task, worth keeping in mind while choosing the drawing: dragging a trim handle moves the playhead, and the playhead is what picks a piece, so a handle drag silently changes which piece Delete would take. The model is right; it just means the pick needs to be legible while a handle is moving.

This surface is retired eventually by a-document-can-have-time, which replaces the strip with a real timeline. Do it anyway: that is days of work away, the user is cutting recordings today, and the lesson (progress must not outshout selection) is one the new timeline lanes inherit.
